summary: Background: GamblingLess: In-The-Moment is an app-based just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI), informed by the Dynamic Model of Relapse, that delivers tailored interventions during moments of cognitive vulnerability to people seeking to reduce or quit gambling. It aims to reduce gambling symptom severity through short-term reductions in gambling episodes (primary proximal outcome) by improving craving intensity, self-efficacy, or positive outcome expectancies (secondary proximal outcomes). Objective: This study aimed to inform the optimization of GamblingLess: In-The-Moment by using a microrandomized trial (MRT) to explore whether tailored interventions, compared with no intervention, reduced subsequent gambling episodes, and improved subsequent craving intensity, self-efficacy, and positive outcome expectancies. A concurrent single-arm outcome evaluation assessed changes in gambling symptom severity (primary distal outcome) and gambling frequency, expenditure, craving severity, self-efficacy, and positive outcome expectancies (secondary distal outcomes) over 6 months. Methods: Australian adults seeking to reduce or quit gambling were recruited using online convenience sampling. In the fully automated, blinded 28-day MRT, participants reporting high craving intensity, low self-efficacy, and/or high positive outcome expectancies in ecological momentary assessments (EMAs), delivered by push notification 3 times daily, were randomized to a tailored intervention or a no-intervention control. Three modules (Curbing Cravings, Tackling Triggers, and Exploring Expectancies) targeted these cognitive processes; control messages comprised brief encouragement without intervention content. Results: Among 192 participants completing at least one EMA (men: n=127, 66.2%; median age 35, IQR 24-44 years), 5116 EMAs were completed (31.7% compliance). In the MRT, the tailored intervention was no more effective than the control condition in reducing subsequent gambling episodes (odds ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.79-1.38; =.74) or associated expenditure, or in improving secondary proximal outcomes. No intervention module demonstrated clear evidence of reducing gambling episodes or associated expenditure, although Tackling Triggers and Exploring Expectancies produced small improvements in their target processes (self-efficacy and positive outcome expectancies, respectively). Sensitivity analyses, including adjustment for other help-seeking, demonstrated similar findings. Supplementary post hoc analyses not fully preserving decision-point randomization suggested small daily improvement in craving intensity and self-efficacy, and medium-to-large immediate improvements in all secondary proximal outcomes after intervention activities. The single-arm evaluation revealed large improvements in gambling symptom severity at postintervention (b=−11.30, 95% CI −12.96 to −9.64; =−0.96; <.001) and 6 months (b=−12.33, 95% CI −14.01 to −10.66; =−1.04; <.001), with 64.6% (104/161) and 66.5% (105/158) of participants, respectively, showing clinically significant recovery or improvement. Small-to-large improvements were also observed across all secondary distal outcomes at both time points. Conclusions: This study is the first to test a theoretically informed multimodule JITAI targeting dynamic cognitive relapse processes. The findings provide important guidance for optimizing gambling JITAIs and other scalable mobile health interventions delivered during moments of vulnerability in real-world settings, alongside promising distal improvements over an extended follow-up period. Trial Registration: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12622000490774; https://www.anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?id=380757&isClinicalTrial=False International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/38958
title: An App-Delivered Just-in-Time Adaptive Intervention for Gambling in Adults (GamblingLess: In-The-Moment): Microrandomized Optimization Trial and Single-Arm Outcome Evaluation

summary: Background: Generative AI (GenAI), particularly large language models, is increasingly being used in behavioral medicine to provide scalable and personalized support. However, evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remains heterogeneous, and the contribution of generative capabilities beyond therapeutic content and intervention design remains unclear. Objective: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of GenAI-based interventions across behavioral medicine and to characterize the intervention features and trial designs relevant to their clinical evaluation and implementation. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus for RCTs published from January 1, 2020, to March 31, 2026. Eligible studies compared GenAI-based interventions with inactive controls, usual care, nongenerative interventions, or active comparators. The primary outcomes were depressive and anxiety symptoms. Secondary outcomes included affect, engagement, empathy, and therapeutic alliance. Risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2), and certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled Hedges values and 95% CIs. Results: Of the 19,475 records identified, 20 RCTs met the eligibility criteria. Of these, 14 (70%) were at overall high risk of bias, 4 (20%) raised some concerns, and 2 (10%) were at low risk. GenAI-based interventions were associated with a small reduction in depressive symptoms in the primary random-effects analysis (Hedges =−0.21, 95% CI −0.41 to −0.02; ²=63%), although the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) sensitivity analysis yielded a CI that included 0 (95% CI −0.46 to 0.04). Anxiety symptoms did not significantly improve (=−0.14, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.02; ²=63%). Negative affect improved, whereas positive affect did not significantly improve. Point estimates favored larger benefits against waitlist controls, but formal between-subgroup tests did not support differences by comparator type for depression (=.20) or anxiety (=.28). Engagement generally favored GenAI-based interventions. Narrative findings suggested greater empathy compared with rule-based systems, mixed empathy findings compared with human-delivered care, and no clear differences in therapeutic alliance compared with active conversational comparators. Follow-up beyond 3 months was limited, and safety reporting was sparse. The certainty of evidence ranged from low to very low. Conclusions: GenAI-based interventions may provide small, outcome-specific benefits in behavioral medicine, but the available evidence does not establish whether these benefits are attributable specifically to generative capabilities. Effects appear to depend on intervention design, human involvement, comparator selection, and implementation context. Current evidence, therefore, supports viewing GenAI as a design-dependent augmentation tool rather than a standalone therapeutic innovation. Future trials should prioritize active comparators, longer follow-up, and transparent reporting of model characteristics and safety outcomes. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251180679; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251180679
title: Effectiveness of Generative AI–Based Interventions in Behavioral Medicine: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

summary: Background: Multimodal AI may improve clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection and risk stratification by integrating imaging, histopathology, molecular, radiomic, and structured clinical data. Objective: This scoping review aimed to map recent evidence on multimodal AI for prostate cancer diagnosis, staging, prognosis, and treatment personalization, with emphasis on data modalities, fusion strategies, validation, reproducibility, and clinical translation. Its added value is a decision-centered evidence map linking fusion strategy and input burden to clinical task, validation strength, reproducibility, and translational readiness across the prostate cancer pathway. Methods: A PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews)–guided search of IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and SpringerLink was conducted to identify English-language peer-reviewed studies published from January 2021 to December 2025. Eligible studies applied AI to at least 2 data sources for prostate cancer detection, grading, staging, prognosis, recurrence prediction, or treatment selection. Two reviewers screened records and charted clinical tasks, modalities, fusion strategy, validation design, performance, and reproducibility indicators. Results: Twenty-six studies were included. Clinical variables were incorporated in 24 studies, multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in 17 studies, and whole-slide histopathology in 6 studies. Multimodal models usually outperformed unimodal baselines in paired comparisons. including prostate imaging: cancer AI (PI-CAI) performance above the median radiologist area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC; 0.91 vs 0.86) and trimodal positron emission tomography (PET)/MRI/clinical models reporting area under the curve (AUC) values of up to 0.955. The evidence was limited by retrospective designs, small cohorts, geographic concentration, scarce public code, inconsistent calibration reporting, and a lack of prospective workflow validation. Conclusions: Multimodal AI is promising for biopsy triage, grading, staging, prognostication, and treatment selection, but current evidence supports research prioritization rather than routine deployment. Prospective, diverse, transparent, and clinically embedded validation is required before multimodal AI can guide routine prostate cancer decisions.
title: Multimodal AI for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis and Risk Stratification: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Patients after sphincter-preserving surgery (SPS) for rectal cancer often need to manage persistent bowel symptoms during recovery and may experience psychological distress, including loneliness, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Self-compassion interventions have been used among patients with cancer, but research on digital self-compassion interventions for this population, particularly during home-based recovery after discharge, remains limited. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of a WeChat Mini Program–based self-compassion intervention on self-compassion in patients after SPS for rectal cancer. We also examined changes in cancer-related loneliness, anxiety, and depressive symptoms and evaluated intervention feasibility and platform usability. Methods: From September 2025 to February 2026, we conducted a single-center, two-arm, parallel-group, single-blind randomized controlled trial at a tertiary Grade A hospital in Anhui Province, China. A total of 160 patients were randomized 1:1 to the intervention or control group. The intervention group received a 4-week WeChat Mini Program–based self-compassion intervention, and the control group received routine postoperative follow-up. The primary outcome was self-compassion, and secondary outcomes were cancer-related loneliness, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T0), at the end of the intervention (week 4; T1), 4 weeks after the intervention (week 8; T2), and 8 weeks after the intervention (week 12; T3). Intervention feasibility was evaluated based on task completion and platform use. The System Usability Scale (SUS) was used to assess platform usability among intervention-group participants who completed T3. Generalized estimating equations were used to examine between-group differences in changes over time, and multiple imputation was used for sensitivity analysis of missing data. Results: A total of 160 participants were randomized, with 80 in each group. At T1, improvement in self-compassion was greater in the intervention group than in the control group (β=6.13, 95% CI 4.44‐7.82; <.001). This difference remained significant at T2 (β=5.25, 95% CI 3.60‐6.90; <.001) and T3 (β=6.52, 95% CI 4.66‐8.38; <.001). Reductions in cancer-related loneliness, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were also greater in the intervention group at all follow-up time points (all <.001). Results of the multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis were generally consistent with the primary analysis. In the intervention group, 62 of 80 (77.5%) participants completed at least 75% of the training tasks. Among the 52 intervention-group participants who completed T3, the mean SUS score was 74.13 (SD 8.00), above the benchmark of 68. Conclusions: During home-based recovery after SPS for rectal cancer, the intervention group showed greater improvement in self-compassion and greater reductions in cancer-related loneliness, anxiety, and depressive symptoms than the control group, and these between-group differences were observed at T2 and T3. Further multicenter studies with longer follow-up are needed. Trial Registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2500107801; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showprojEN.html?proj=283239
title: Effectiveness of a WeChat-Based Self-Compassion Intervention for Patients After Sphincter-Preserving Surgery for Rectal Cancer: Randomized Controlled Trial
How Emerging Technology Is Changing Our Relationship With Memory

summary: Background: Single-camera markerless motion capture systems (MLMCS) offer a low-cost, portable alternative to marker-based motion capture systems (MBMCS) for lower-limb assessment, but the evidence remains fragmented across movement tasks, algorithms, and validation frameworks. Existing reviews have addressed broader health care applications, disease-specific gait technologies, or general pose-estimation use cases, but a focused synthesis of monocular two-dimensional (2D) and 3D red-green-blue (RGB)-camera MLMCS for human lower-limb activities has been lacking. Objective: This scoping review aimed to map how single RGB-camera MLMCS have been used to quantify lower-limb kinematics by examining data collection protocols, participant/task characteristics, computational pipelines, human pose estimation (HPE) methods, and reference standards and validation strategies. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidance, we searched PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, CINAHL, and SPORTDiscus from database inception to March 16, 2026. Peer-reviewed English-language studies of human lower-limb activities using a single RGB camera were eligible. Two reviewers (BG and DH) independently screened studies and appraised quality using a modified Downs and Black checklist. Findings were synthesized descriptively. Results: Out of a total of 4484 identified records, 39 studies were included. The evidence base was dominated by gait-related tasks (29/39, 75%) and predominantly healthy cohorts, with knee flexion/extension and hip flexion/extension as the most frequently reported outcomes. Twenty-five distinct MLMCS methods were identified. OpenPose (Perceptual Computing Lab) was the most frequently used 2D approach. Across studies, performance was most consistent for sagittal-plane hip and knee flexion/extension, whereas ankle plantarflexion/dorsiflexion, frontal- and transverse-plane kinematics, and occluded-side estimation remained less robust and less consistently validated. Unlike broader previous reviews, this review provides the first focused evidence map of monocular RGB lower-limb applications across tasks, populations, hardware/software configurations, HPE algorithms, and benchmarking strategies. It also offers a clearer performance hierarchy, with OpenPose emerging as the strongest 2D option for sagittal knee flexion/extension and the World-grounded Humans with Accurate Motion (WHAM) method as the best-performing single-view 3D system overall in the largest benchmark. Conclusions: This review advances the field by clarifying where single RGB-camera MLMCS are currently most credible and where major limitations remain. In real-world settings, these systems show promise as accessible tools for repeated movement assessment, screening, and longitudinal monitoring when the primary target is sagittal-plane hip and knee motion. However, broader clinical deployment will require more standardized protocols, richer ankle and foot keypoint definitions, pathology-specific validation, and greater robustness to occlusion, viewpoint variation, and real-world recording conditions.
title: Monocular Two-Dimensional and 3D Red-Green-Blue-Camera Marker-Less Motion Capture Systems for Human Lower-Limb Activities: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Pregnancy risk assessment requires not only accurate identification of risk but also communication, referral, and follow-up across different levels of care. Although AI-based tools are increasingly proposed to support this process, evidence remains limited on how women, primary health care professionals, and hospital-based maternity care providers expect AI-generated risk information to be interpreted and used in care, as well as on what conditions they consider important for its practical use. Objective: This study aimed to explore multistakeholder expectations and anticipated implementation concerns regarding AI-based pregnancy risk assessment in maternity care, with particular attention to how AI-generated risk information could be interpreted, confirmed, and used to inform care decisions and subsequent management. Methods: This qualitative descriptive study used semistructured interviews with 93 participants in Guizhou Province, China, including 33 (33.5%) pregnant or postpartum women, 23 (24.7%) primary health care professionals, and 37 (39.8%) hospital-based maternity care providers. Purposive sampling with maximum variation was used. Participants were recruited from 18 health care facilities, including primary health care facilities and secondary and tertiary hospitals. Interviews were conducted between August 30, 2024, and May 2026. Brief standardized conceptual material was used to support discussion of AI-based pregnancy risk assessment; it did not depict a specific product or prototype. Data were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis. Results: Five descriptive themes and 16 subthemes were developed. The expected value of AI-based pregnancy risk assessment depended on whether it addressed practical gaps in pregnancy risk management, although priorities differed across stakeholder groups. Women emphasized understandable risk information and care-seeking guidance; primary health care professionals emphasized referral, feedback, and follow-up continuity; and hospital-based providers valued clinically interpretable information for assessment, management, and cross-level coordination. Participants valued early and dynamic risk recognition because pregnancy risk could emerge, worsen, or be reclassified as pregnancy progressed, making sustained visibility of risk information important. AI-generated risk information was not treated as self-evident; it needed to be interpreted and confirmed in relation to women’s bodily experience, clinicians’ judgment, examination results, referral rules, and higher-level confirmation. Risk recognition was considered useful when it could be translated into guidance, referral, feedback, and follow-up. Implementation concerns centered on risk communication and anxiety management for women and on workload, usability, training, and organizational support for health care professionals. Conclusions: Stakeholders expected AI-based pregnancy risk assessment to provide risk information that could become meaningful and actionable within existing maternity care pathways. Future AI tools in maternity care should therefore be evaluated not only for predictive accuracy but also for whether risk information can be understood, communicated, confirmed, and carried forward into follow-up and coordinated action across levels of care.
title: Multistakeholder Expectations and Implementation Concerns Regarding AI-Based Pregnancy Risk Assessment in Maternity Care: Qualitative Descriptive Study

summary: Background: HIV cure research has advanced since the first reported cure case in 2008, but confirmed cure outcomes remain extremely rare. Community discussions on platforms such as Reddit’s r/hivaids both reflect and shape perceptions of cure research, stigma, and willingness to participate in studies. Understanding this online dialogue is therefore critical for optimizing outreach, education, and information strategies. Objective: The goal of our study was to determine whether social listening methods can characterize the scope, patterns, and content of online discourse about HIV cure and cure-directed research within a social media community. Methods: We conducted a social listening analysis of more than 142,000 posts from 12,227 authors on r/hivaids (2011‐2025). Using natural language processing, we characterized communication themes and engagement patterns and evaluated how discussion volume related to trends in the scientific publication landscape. User geography was inferred from self-disclosed information in posts and comments. Results: Location analysis showed overrepresentation from North America, consistent with Reddit’s largely US‑based user population (approximately 49.6% of daily users), and limited participation from high‑burden regions such as Africa and Asia. “Cure” was the most common term, whereas more specific research language (eg, “remission” or “functional cure”) was rarely used. Cure‑related discussion volume closely paralleled the appearance of new scientific reports rather than general news cycles. Thematic analysis identified “hope for a cure” as the dominant topic, with frequent positive and optimistic themes—particularly among non‑US users. In contrast, US‑based posts more often included limited content on research details and policy (eg, profitability and funding for HIV cure research, clinical trials, bone marrow transplantation, a vaccine, etc), while non‑US posts also highlighted mental health challenges, optimism after diagnosis, and ongoing social issues such as stigma and discrimination. Only 16% (743/4644) of cure‑related posts referenced cure-directed research directly. Engagement was highly concentrated among a small number of “nano‑influencer” users. Conclusions: Online HIV cure and HIV cure–directed research discussions on Reddit are largely optimistic, use relatively simple language, and show engagement peaks that align with new scientific data rather than general news cycles. These conversations also vary markedly by geography. Closing language gaps, strategically partnering with key community influencers, and extending outreach into high-burden regions should be priorities to maximize global impact.
title: Patterns of HIV Cure and HIV Cure–Directed Research Discussions in an Online Community Over 14 Years: Global Social Listening Approach

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> A growing number of US adults and youth confide in generative AI chatbots for mental health support, including disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. While chatbot response quality, safety, and effectiveness could impact population-level suicide and self-harm rates, there are no systematic reviews of this burgeoning literature. <strong>Objective:</strong> We conducted a systematic review of studies evaluating generative AI chatbot responses to disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. <strong>Methods:</strong> We followed PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 and PRISMA-S (PRISMA literature search extension) guidelines and preregistered the protocol on the Open Science Framework. We included English-language, peer-reviewed publications and preprints from 2020 to 2025 that empirically evaluated generative AI conversational responses to suicidal ideation, suicidal or nonsuicidal self-harm, or suicide-planning content. Eligible designs included audits, chatbot development, and adversarial “jailbreaking” studies. We excluded nongenerative systems, clinician-training tools, and prediction-only models. The final database searches were run from December 18 to 23, 2025 (PubMed, Embase, APA PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and OSF Preprints). On July 26, 2026, publication status was rechecked to update preprint vs published classification. After deduplication, titles/abstracts and full texts were independently screened by 2 reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Methodological quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018. We conducted a narrative synthesis across 7 safety domains and 5 AI classifications (proprietary, open-weight, companions, clinical, and study-specific). <strong>Results:</strong> Of 1042 deduplicated records, 126 full texts were reviewed, and 29 were included (16 published; 13 preprints). Most studies evaluated suicidal content only (21/29). Twenty were solely audit studies, 2 chatbot development, and 1 jailbreaking. The rest combined approaches. Most used synthetic, single-turn prompts; only 6 used multiturn conversations. Most studies evaluated ≥2 of our 5 AI classifications (17/29). Proprietary models were included most frequently (23/29). When compared, proprietary models (eg, ChatGPT and Claude) tended to provide higher-quality responses than open-weight models (eg, Llama and DeepSeek) and many companions (eg, Replika and Character.AI); however, this trend weakened with sensitivity analysis. Chatbots generally performed well on emotional support, but responses were often generic and lacked context. Chatbots rarely assessed suicide or self-harm risk and performed most poorly when disclosure was ambiguous or moderate. Responses were inconsistent, often requiring multiple turns before referral to crisis resources or human support. Overtly harmful responses were rare under standard conditions but common under jailbreaking. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Evidence is limited by the proportion of preprints, variable quality, synthetic single-turn prompts, small samples, heterogeneous outcomes, and rapid model versioning. Nonetheless, current chatbots tend to provide validation but struggle to escalate care, assess risk, and resist jailbreaking. Research is needed on stakeholder perspectives and on the short- and long-term clinical impact of chatbot responses using follow-up assessments in real-world or clinical settings. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registries osf.io/7fz95; https://osf.io/7fz95
title: Generative AI Chatbot Responses to Suicide and Self-Harm: Systematic Review

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Postinfectious bone loss can lead to spinal instability and severe neurological complications, with potentially devastating outcomes. However, prognostic models to support individualized risk assessment remain limited. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and internally validate a visual nomogram integrating multimodal clinical data to estimate postinfectious bone loss risk in patients with spinal infection and inform individualized monitoring strategies. <strong>Methods:</strong> This retrospective cohort study used consecutive sampling at Shandong Public Health Clinical Center. Baseline clinical and laboratory data were extracted from medical records. Eligible patients had confirmed spinal infection, a baseline vertebral bone destruction height ratio less than one-third, and complete baseline and follow-up data. Postinfectious bone loss was defined as a height ratio greater than or equal to one-third on computed tomography 12 months after baseline. Predictors were selected from 31 baseline variables using univariable logistic regression followed by least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Multivariable logistic regression was used to construct the nomogram. Internal validation used 500 bootstrap resamples, repeating all predictor selection and model-fitting steps. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, the Brier score, decision curve analysis, and clinical impact curve analysis. <strong>Results:</strong> Postinfectious bone loss occurred in 48.9% (109/223, 95% CI 42.4%-55.4%) of patients. The nomogram combined infection characteristics (multidrug-resistant bacterial infection and infected spinal segment), skeletal status (osteoporosis), and laboratory markers (interleukin-6, albumin, and plasma fibrinogen) to estimate individual risk. In the multivariable model, the odds ratios (ORs) were 2.718 (95% CI 0.993-7.444; <i>P</i>=.05) for multidrug-resistant bacterial infection and 7.345 (95% CI 2.757-19.570; <i>P</i><.001) for osteoporosis. Relative to cervical infection, ORs were 14.041 (95% CI 1.079-182.662; <i>P</i>=.04) for thoracic, 28.876 (95% CI 2.648-314.895; <i>P</i>=.006) for lumbar, and 12.604 (95% CI 0.436-364.075; <i>P</i>=.14) for thoracolumbar infection. Per unit increase, ORs were 1.004 (95% CI 0.996-1.012; <i>P</i>=.30) for interleukin-6 (pg/mL), 3.673 (95% CI 2.410-5.598; <i>P</i><.001) for plasma fibrinogen (g/L), and 0.834 (95% CI 0.749-0.929; <i>P</i>=.001) for albumin (g/L). Discrimination remained high after optimism correction, with an AUC of 0.946 (95% CI 0.919-0.972), compared with an apparent AUC of 0.954 (95% CI 0.931-0.978). Calibration assessment yielded an intercept of 0.00 (95% CI –0.43 to 0.43) and a slope of 1.00 (95% CI 0.75-1.25), while the Brier score was 0.096 (95% CI 0.064-0.118), indicating close agreement between predicted and observed risks and low overall prediction error. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study developed a visual nomogram integrating baseline clinical characteristics, imaging features, and laboratory parameters to predict postinfectious bone loss in patients with spinal infection. Extending previous association studies to individualized risk prediction, the model showed good discrimination and calibration in internal validation. This approach may help identify high-risk patients and inform closer monitoring and timely reassessment before further structural deterioration and neurological complications.
title: Integrating Multidimensional Clinical Data to Develop a Visual Nomogram for Individualized Prediction of Postinfectious Bone Loss in Patients With Spinal Infection: Retrospective Cohort Study
